strengths: Novel end-to-end architecture that unifies feed-forward inverse rendering (MVSplat), a transformer-only dynamics model built on PTv3 with a new temporal serialization/merging scheme, and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering, trained purely from multi-view RGB with an image reconstruction loss — avoiding privileged signals (depth, particle tracks, hand-crafted graphs) used by most prior particle-based simulators.

The temporal extension of PTv3 (temporally serialized point clouds, learned temporal positional encoding, and temporal merging via bit-shifting of serialization codes) is a reasonably original technical contribution that replaces expensive kNN-based graph construction with scalable, hardware-friendly attention.

Extensive ablation studies (rollout length, camera count, segmentation mask necessity, input modality configuration, grid resolution, and temporal merger design) give useful insight into design choices and their effect on performance, which aids reproducibility and understanding of the method's sensitivities.

Qualitative demonstrations of generalization beyond training distribution (novel multi-body interactions, scene edits such as ground removal/height changes, emergent shadow modeling) are compelling and suggest the learned representation captures more than narrow next-frame prediction.

The paper is transparent about missing baselines (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys lack public code/data) and commits to releasing code and datasets, which would meaningfully aid reproducibility in a subfield that currently lacks open baselines.

Reasonably clear presentation of the architecture with helpful figures (Fig. 4-6) breaking down the temporal encoding/merging pipeline, and a well-organized related-work table (Table 1) situating the contribution.
weaknesses: The only external quantitative baseline is Cosmos, a 2D single-view video generation model not designed for multi-view 3D particle simulation; this is an unfair/mismatched comparison (different task setup, different conditioning) and does not substitute for comparison against actual particle-based simulator baselines, even partial or adapted versions of open-source methods like DPI-Net.

All experiments are conducted on synthetic datasets generated by the authors (GSO rigid bodies, Genesis MPM elastic/cloth) with only 6 objects per category and single simple scenes (object falling on a ground plane/cloth); there is no validation on real-world video, which is explicitly deferred to future work and substantially limits the claimed significance for real embodied-AI applications discussed in the introduction.

Key qualitative claims (multi-body generalization retaining structural integrity, physically plausible generalization to unseen scene edits, emergent shadow modeling) are supported only by a handful of illustrative examples without quantitative metrics or systematic evaluation, so their generality and robustness are unclear.

The comparison table (Table 2 on p.8) largely compares internal variants of 3DGSim itself (explicit vs. latent, 2 vs 4 past steps, with/without masks) rather than against competing methods, so the paper's central claim of superiority/advance over prior particle-based simulators is not empirically substantiated beyond narrative argument.

Some ablation results are inconsistent or counterintuitive without clear explanation (e.g., Table S3 shows removing segmentation masks improves PSNR-past considerably, and Table S6 shows large performance swings from merging timing that are not fully analyzed mechanistically).

Training requires ~5 days on a single H100 GPU with large batch/rollout requirements, which combined with the lack of released code at submission time (promised but not yet available) limits immediate reproducibility.

The physical interpretation offered (e.g., 'transformer avoids structural constraints that limit generalization' for multi-body scenes) is speculative and not rigorously tested via ablation or controlled comparison to GNN-based alternatives on the same data.

strengths: The architectural contribution is coherent and reasonably novel: replacing kNN/GNN-based particle dynamics with a transformer operating on space-filling-curve serialized point clouds (extending PTv3), combined with a temporal encoding/merging scheme that allows reuse of the same attention blocks across timesteps rather than per-timestep modules as in prior work (e.g., HD-VPD). This is a sensible engineering contribution that removes some hand-crafted biases.

The end-to-end training of inverse rendering (MVSplat-based), dynamics prediction, and 3DGS rendering purely from an image reconstruction loss (no privileged depth/tracks) is a reasonable and relevant research direction for scalable visuo-physical learning.

The paper includes fairly extensive ablations (rollout length, camera count, segmentation masks, modality configuration, grid resolution, temporal merger design) which is useful for understanding design choices, even if restricted to a single dataset.

Qualitative results span three distinct physical regimes (rigid, elastic, cloth) and show visually plausible behavior, including some interesting emergent effects (shadow modeling, boundary constraints on cloth).

The authors commit to releasing code and data, which is valuable given that several cited baselines (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) are closed-source, a genuine gap in the field that this could help address.
weaknesses: No comparison to any real particle-based dynamics baseline (GNN-based or otherwise) despite an entire related-work table built around such comparisons; the only quantitative comparison is to Cosmos, a pretrained single-view video generation model conditioned on language prompts, which is explicitly acknowledged as 'not directly comparable' to the multi-view particle-based setup. This leaves the paper's central claim -- that removing relational/graph biases in favor of a transformer-only design is beneficial -- essentially unsubstantiated by controlled experiments.

All experiments are on small-scale, synthetic datasets (6 objects per category, <=1000 trajectories, <6 minutes of footage per object), which directly contradicts the paper's stated motivation of targeting 'data-rich regimes' where inductive biases supposedly hurt scalability. No real-world validation is provided, and this is acknowledged only briefly as future work.

Several striking qualitative claims (multi-body generalization, scene editing, shadow modeling, 'robust understanding of physics beyond training distribution') are supported only by a handful of qualitative frames/figures with no quantitative metrics, human evaluation, or failure-rate analysis; some of the shown examples (objects sinking through the table in Fig. 10) actually reflect failure modes framed positively.

Ablations are conducted exclusively on the elastic dataset, so conclusions about hyperparameters (grid resolution, temporal merger schedule, camera counts) may not generalize to the rigid or cloth settings that the paper also reports on.

The reported PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS numbers lack a meaningful frame of reference: there is no comparison to the underlying MVSplat reconstruction quality without dynamics, nor to a simple baseline (e.g., static/no-motion prediction, optical-flow warping) that would clarify how much of the gain is attributable to genuine dynamics modeling versus rendering quality alone.

The claim of a 'transformer-only' or 'minimal-bias' design is somewhat overstated: the method still relies on hand-tuned grid resolution, serialization/patch-size choices, masking/freezing heuristics, and camera-view selection, several of which are shown in the ablations to be fragile (e.g., explicit representation collapsing to planar artifacts with fewer views, failure at 2/4 cameras), undercutting the 'scalability over inductive bias' narrative.

Camera setup ablations (Table S2) show that with very limited views training fails entirely, and explicit representations are highly unstable; this fragility is not deeply analyzed and raises concerns about real-world applicability where dense multi-view capture (12 cameras) is often impractical.

Statistical treatment is thin: reported means ± std across small held-out sets (12% of trajectories from small datasets) with overlapping error bars in several comparisons (e.g., latent vs explicit variants) are treated as meaningfully different without significance testing.

strengths: Genuine architectural novelty: replaces the GNN+kNN paradigm dominant in prior particle-based simulators with a transformer-only dynamics engine using space-filling curve serialization (extending PTv3) and a Temporal Merging module, avoiding hand-crafted graph construction and privileged 3D signals (depth, particle tracks).

Fully end-to-end differentiable pipeline that unifies feed-forward inverse rendering (MVSplat-based), particle dynamics, and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering, trained purely from multi-view RGB reconstruction loss -- a meaningful simplification relative to prior NeRF/GNN-based approaches.

Extensive and informative ablation study (Appendix B) covering rollout length, camera count, segmentation mask reliance, input modality configurations, grid resolution, and temporal merging strategy, which clarifies design choices and their sensitivity.

Qualitative results are compelling: the model generalizes to unseen multi-body interactions, scene edits (ground removal/height change), and produces plausible secondary effects like shadows purely from learned features, suggesting the representation captures more than narrow training signal.

The paper is transparent about the difficulty of benchmarking against closed-source/no-data prior works (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) and commits to releasing code and datasets, which would provide a useful reproducible baseline for the community.
Clear, well-structured writing with detailed architectural diagrams and a helpful literature positioning table (Table 1).
weaknesses: No real-world validation: all experiments are on synthetic data (GSO rigid bodies, Genesis MPM elastic/cloth objects), explicitly acknowledged as a 'proof of concept.' This is a significant gap given the paper's central motivation is scalability to real, data-rich video regimes.

The training data is limited in diversity (6 objects per dataset category, <6 minutes of footage per object), which sits awkwardly against the introduction's emphasis on 'data-rich regimes' as the paper's key differentiator from GNN methods -- the actual data scale tested is small.

The only quantitative dynamics baseline is Cosmos, a single-view pretrained video generation model that is explicitly noted as 'not directly comparable' to the multi-view particle-based setup; there is no quantitative comparison to any of the closest prior particle-based simulators (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys, GNN-based methods), even via reduced/adapted reimplementation, weakening claims of superiority or even parity with the graph-based inductive-bias approaches it argues against.

The paper's most interesting claims -- physically plausible generalization to novel multi-body interactions, scene edits, and emergent shadow modeling -- are supported only qualitatively (figures, supplementary video) without any quantitative metric or user study, making it hard to assess robustness or cherry-picking.

Central claims regarding the necessity/superiority of dropping GNN/kNN inductive biases are argued primarily through comparison to a non-graph-based baseline (Cosmos) rather than through a controlled ablation against a GNN-based dynamics model trained under the same pipeline, leaving the core hypothesis of the paper only indirectly tested.

Some ablation results (e.g., camera setup, temporal merger) are based on relatively short training budgets (80k-85k of ~120k steps) and a single dataset (elastic only), limiting generality of the conclusions drawn.

strengths: Novel, well-motivated architecture that combines feed-forward multi-view inverse rendering (MVSplat), a transformer-only dynamics engine extending PTv3 with a Temporal Encoding & Merging (TEM) module, and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering into a single end-to-end differentiable pipeline, avoiding costly kNN/graph construction used in prior GNN-based particle simulators.

Extensive and systematic ablation studies (main paper Table 1 plus supplementary Sections C.1-C.6) probing rollout length, camera setup, segmentation masking, grid resolution, input modality, and especially the temporal merger design, which convincingly demonstrate the necessity of the TEM module (removing it causes a ~15 dB PSNR collapse) and the latent-vs-explicit representation choice.

Compelling qualitative demonstrations of out-of-distribution generalization (ground removal, higher drops, multi-object interactions with up to 5 objects) despite training only on single-object collisions, with clear qualitative contrasts against a 2D video baseline (CosmosFT) that hallucinates levitation and object merging.

Reasonably honest treatment of baseline comparison limitations: the authors explain why several particle-based simulator baselines (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) cannot be compared due to lack of released code/data, and they transparently discuss the caveats of the Spring-Gaus and PhysDreamer comparisons rather than hiding them.

Inclusion of preliminary real-world results on the HO-Cap dataset (action-conditioned hand-object manipulation) extends the method beyond synthetic data and includes an interesting failure-mode analysis showing that the model's causal, spatially-grounded design avoids hallucinating continued object motion once hand particles degrade.

Clear ablation-driven design rationale (e.g., FiLM-based view-independent feature encoding, invariant/dynamic feature decomposition, space-filling curve serialization) that is grounded in prior work (PTv3, MVSplat) but meaningfully extended for the temporal/dynamics setting.
weaknesses: Training datasets are small and narrow in scope (six objects per category, less than 6 minutes of footage per object, single-object-ground collisions only), raising concerns about how well the reported generalization would hold at larger scale or with more diverse real scenes; the real-world HO-Cap evaluation is similarly small (64 trajectories) and only action-conditioned rather than passive.

Quantitative evaluation of the paper's most striking claims (OOD generalization to ground removal, multi-object interactions, shadow emergence) is entirely qualitative; no numerical metrics are reported for these scenarios, making it hard to assess robustness or cherry-picking risk.

The lack of comparison to actual particle-based/GNN simulators (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) — the closest prior work in spirit — is a significant gap; while the authors give a plausible explanation (no released code/data), this leaves the central claim of the paper (that graph-free transformer dynamics can match or surpass GNN-based PBS) empirically unverified against the most relevant literature.

Evaluation relies solely on image-based reconstruction metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD) rather than any 3D/physical-state accuracy metric; while the authors provide a rationale (particle correspondence is ill-defined), this makes it difficult to disentangle rendering quality from genuine dynamics/physics accuracy.

Reported failure modes (blurring/drift of hand particles beyond ~4s in real-world rollouts, degraded performance with fewer cameras or mismatched input-window lengths at inference) indicate meaningful robustness limitations that are not fully resolved or quantified across the main experimental suite.

Training cost is substantial (~6 days on a single H100 GPU per configuration), and combined with the large number of hyperparameters/architectural components (TEM strides, grid size, rollout length, patch size, etc.), reproducibility by other groups without the exact code release may be challenging despite the promised open-source release.

The comparisons against Spring-Gaus and Cosmos, while transparently caveated, are somewhat apples-to-oranges (different input requirements, per-trajectory optimization vs. feed-forward, no visual/lighting modeling for Spring-Gaus), limiting how much these results can be used to support superiority claims.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely novel end-to-end differentiable pipeline (MVSplat encoder + transformer-only PTv3-based dynamics with a temporal encoding/merging mechanism + 3D Gaussian rendering) that removes hand-crafted graph biases (kNN, edges) used in prior GNN-based particle simulators, which is a meaningful architectural contribution.

Extensive ablation studies are provided (TEM removal, rollout length, latent vs. explicit representation, camera count, segmentation masks, grid resolution, modality configurations, temporal merger schedule), giving good insight into which design choices matter.

Qualitative OOD generalization demonstrations (ground removal, increased drop height, multi-object interactions with objects unseen in combination) are compelling and illustrate a genuine advantage of an explicit 3D/particle representation over the 2D video baseline (CosmosFT), which hallucinates levitation and object merging.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough, including detailed discussion contrasting the method with dynamic scene reconstruction (4DGS) and analytical-simulator-based methods (PhysGaussian, PhysDreamer, Spring-Gaus), a rationale for image-based metrics, and failure-mode analysis on real data.

Preliminary real-world results on HO-Cap, though limited, show an attempt to move beyond purely synthetic data and highlight an interpretable failure mode (interaction ceases when hand particles fade) that supports the claim of learned spatial causality rather than pixel hallucination.

Authors are transparent about baseline limitations (no code/data available for closest prior GNN-PBS works despite author requests) and about caveats in the Spring-Gauss comparison, which is commendable honesty even though it leaves an evaluation gap.
weaknesses: The core quantitative claim of "physically plausible" and "competitive" simulation rests almost entirely on image-based reconstruction metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD); there is no quantitative measurement of trajectory or positional accuracy against ground-truth physical state, so it is hard to verify whether the model is learning physics versus learning to render plausible-looking but physically inaccurate motion, especially over longer horizons.

No comparison against any of the closest and most relevant prior particle-based simulators (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys, DPI-Net, VGPLDP) is actually performed; the paper only argues these are infeasible to reproduce. This leaves the central claim of outperforming/complementing prior 3D particle simulators largely unsubstantiated by direct evidence.

The training datasets are small and narrow: only 6 objects per category (rigid, elastic, cloth), less than 6 minutes of footage per object, single-object-ground collision scenarios only. Generalization claims (multi-object, ground removal) are demonstrated only qualitatively on a handful of cherry-picked examples with no quantitative evaluation or systematic study of failure rates.

The real-world validation (HO-Cap) substantially deviates from the proposed method: MVSplat is replaced by a pretrained DepthAnything3 model, the encoder is only fine-tuned rather than trained end-to-end from scratch, and evaluation is action-conditioned rather than passive multi-view video as claimed to be the paper's target setting. This undermines the generality claims for the actual method described in the main text.

Some ablation comparisons appear confounded by inconsistent training budgets (e.g., Table S8's best temporal-merger configuration is trained for 120k steps while all others are trained for 80k steps), making it unclear whether the reported gains are due to the architectural choice or simply more training.

The dramatic performance collapse when removing TEM (33.15 → 18.19 PSNR) is presented without deeper analysis of why simple spatial-only attention fails so catastrophically, raising questions about whether the comparison is fully controlled (e.g., equal parameter count, comparable receptive field).

Training cost is high (~6 days on a single H100 per model) and inference speed for the full system is modest (12–20 FPS), which limits practical significance for robotics/embodied applications the paper motivates itself with.

The Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate non-statement ("none which we feel must be specifically highlighted"), despite the paper explicitly targeting embodied/robotics applications where safety and misuse considerations (e.g., simulated dynamics used for real-world manipulation) would merit at least brief discussion.

The claim that the model encodes physical properties (mass, friction, material) into latent features is asserted repeatedly but never empirically probed or validated (e.g., no linear probing of latent features against known material parameters), making this a central but unverified claim of the paper.

strengths: Novel end-to-end differentiable architecture that unifies feed-forward inverse rendering (MVSplat), a transformer-only particle dynamics model, and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering, trained solely via an image reconstruction loss -- removing the kNN/graph construction overhead that the paper shows dominates forward-time cost in prior GNN-based particle simulators.

The proposed Temporal Encoding and Merging (TEM) module is a genuinely useful extension of PTv3 to spatio-temporal point clouds, enabling variable-length input windows with a single shared attention stack (rather than per-timestep models as in prior work); the ablation showing its removal collapses PSNR from ~33 to ~18 is a convincing demonstration of its necessity.

Extensive and carefully designed ablation studies (main paper Table 1 plus ~10 supplementary ablations covering rollout length, camera count, grid resolution, merging strides, latent vs. explicit representation, segmentation masking) that substantiate individual design choices rather than just reporting an aggregate number.

Compelling qualitative evidence of out-of-distribution generalization (ground removal, multi-object duplication despite single-object training, emergent shadow rendering) that is directly contrasted with clear failure modes of a strong 2D video-generation baseline (CosmosFT), illustrating the practical benefit of the 3D spatial-causality inductive bias.

Honest and detailed discussion of baseline limitations (e.g., Spring-Gauss requiring privileged inputs and per-trajectory optimization, inaccessibility of prior 3D PBS codebases) and of the paper's own limitations (particle correspondence issues, real-world dependence on pretrained monocular priors, degradation under long autoregressive rollouts), including a dedicated failure-case analysis on real-world data.

Preliminary but non-trivial extension to real-world, action-conditioned HO-Cap data, including quantitative rollout-stability analysis against a constant-frame baseline, which strengthens the paper's applicability claims beyond purely synthetic settings.
Commitment to open-source code and dataset release, supporting reproducibility for a research direction where most prior particle-based simulators are closed-source.
weaknesses: Quantitative comparisons to genuine 3D particle-based baselines are thin: most prior GNN/graph-based PBS methods cannot be compared due to lack of released code, and the two baselines that are run (Spring-Gauss, Cosmos) both have substantial, self-acknowledged caveats (privileged inputs / per-trajectory optimization for Spring-Gauss; a general-purpose 2D model not architected for this task for Cosmos), leaving the core simulation-accuracy claims only loosely benchmarked against directly comparable prior work.

Evaluation relies exclusively on image-space metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD); while the rationale given (non-unique particle correspondence) is reasonable, it means physical/dynamical accuracy is only assessed indirectly through rendering fidelity, and OOD generalization claims (multi-object interactions, ground removal) are supported only qualitatively with no quantitative metric, making them somewhat anecdotal.

Training data per object is very limited (<6 minutes of video, 6 objects per category, synthetic scenes for the main results), and the only real-world validation (HO-Cap) uses just 64 trajectories and a substituted pretrained monocular depth backbone rather than the proposed multi-view MVSplat encoder trained from scratch -- this somewhat undercuts the central claim of learning directly from raw multi-view RGB and leaves open how well the method scales to more diverse, larger-scale real scenes.

Reported training cost (~120k steps, ~6 days on a single H100) is substantial, and combined with the narrow per-object data regime, raises questions about practical scalability and reproducibility for groups without comparable compute.

Most ablations (Table 1 and Appendix C) are conducted only on the elastic dataset; it is unclear whether the same trends (e.g., TEM criticality, optimal grid size/merging schedule) hold uniformly across the rigid and cloth regimes, which behave quite differently physically.

Long-horizon autoregressive rollouts show clear degradation (particle blur/drift in HO-Cap results after ~4s), and while this is disclosed candidly, it suggests the method's long-term stability guarantees are limited, particularly for more complex, articulated real-world interactions.
